theme: Sing to the LORD a new song, his salvation revealed
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 98. You will read it again later in the plan. Read it now as the song that follows the judgment: the nations see the salvation of God.
settingTheScene: Psalm 98 is another royal psalm with a new song. Its last verses mirror Psalm 96. Isaac Watts based “Joy to the World” on this psalm, though he reapplied it to the coming of Christ. For the returned exiles, it carried a message: the God who has brought us home will be seen by the whole world.
observation: “Oh sing to the LORD a new song, for he has done marvelous things!” (v. 1).
“His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him” (v. 1).
“The LORD has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations” (v. 2).
“He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel” (v. 3).
“All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God” (v. 3).
“Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth into joyous song and sing praises!” (v. 4).
“Let the rivers clap their hands; let the hills sing for joy together” (vv. 8).
“For he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity” (v. 9).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with a new song, because God has done something new. The language of verse 1 is like Isaiah’s: his right hand and holy arm have worked salvation. This was the language of the exodus. It is a God who saves, not a God who waits to be saved.

The key is verses 2 and 3. “He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel.” God is not forgetful. After the exile, the people had wondered if he had forgotten them. The answer is that he has remembered. And the result is for the whole earth: “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.” God’s saving acts for Israel are meant to be visible to all nations. This is the universal side of God’s choice of Israel.

The music rises. A joyful noise, then a whole orchestra: lyre, trumpets, horn. The sea roars and the rivers clap their hands. The hills sing for joy. Creation joins because the Lord is coming. And the reason is judgment: “He will judge the world with righteousness.” Again, judgment is a cause for rejoicing. If the judge is righteous, it means that the world will be set right.

In this psalm the coming of the LORD has a double face. For Israel, it is salvation and remembrance of love. For the nations, it is the revelation of his righteousness. For creation, it is the end of groaning. For those who trust him, it is the greatest joy.

When Isaac Watts wrote “Joy to the World,” he saw in this psalm the coming of Christ. “Let earth receive her King.” It is a faithful reading. The one whose salvation was revealed to the nations came as a baby in Bethlehem, and he will come again.
connection: Luke 2:30-32: Simeon said, “My eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles.” Luke 1:54-55 says God has remembered his mercy. Romans 8:19-21: creation waits with eager longing. Acts 17:31: God will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed. Revelation 5:9: they sang a new song. Isaiah 52:10: all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.
application:
Sing a hymn today, such as “Joy to the World,” and think of the psalm behind it.

Ask: what “marvelous thing” has God done for you recently? Write it as a new song or a short note.

Pray for the ends of the earth to see his salvation.
prayerPrompts: Sing to the LORD a new song, in your own words.
Thank him for the salvation he has revealed.
Ask him to help you make a joyful noise.
